puzzles.description: Talk with the Agent in the War Room

config.name: The Agent
config.greeting: Hey! Great to meet you. I'm your AI partner for this Bolt. The PO gave us a brief — "I want a customer feedback portal." That's one line. I've already drafted full specs from it — three user stories with who/what/why. Before we build anything, I'd love you to verify them. AI proposes, you decide — yeah?

lines.label: What's a Bolt?
lines.response: In AI-DLC, a Bolt is one full loop — Intent → Plan → Verify → Build → Verify → Ship — done in hours, not weeks. We've got fifteen minutes for this one. Plenty of time, if we don't single-shot it.

lines.label: Why do we need to verify your specs?
lines.response: Because I'm fast, not infallible. The PO gave one sentence; I expanded that into a full spec. For each user story I generated plausible-looking who/what/why options. Some are spot-on. Some I made up. Hallucinations are normal — that's exactly why we have a human-verify step.

lines.label: How should we approach this?
lines.response: Talk to the PO first to lock in actual intent. Then open the Spec Board and walk each story's who/what/why. For each field, pick the option that matches what the PO actually asked for. Reject the inventions.

state_lines.label: We caught the hallucinations.
state_lines.response: Great catch. Three specs validated, every who/what/why grounded in what the PO actually said. The Design Lab door is open — let's load my memory with the right docs next. I'll propose, you verify. Same loop.

config.name: The PO
config.greeting: Right — I want a customer feedback portal. Customers submit feedback, our support team reads it, customers know we received it. That's it. Don't over-build.

lines.label: What exactly do customers do?
lines.response: They submit feedback. Short comments. We give them a confirmation that we got it. That's the whole loop from their side.

lines.label: What does the support team need?
lines.response: They need to read incoming feedback and spot patterns over time. A simple admin view. No fancy analytics. Not yet.

lines.label: Anything we should NOT build?
lines.response: Do not auto-post anything to social media. Do not, under any circumstances, do anything with cryptocurrency. Do not track customer locations. If your AI suggests any of those, ignore it — it's hallucinating.

lines.label: When do you need this live?
lines.response: End of Bolt. Fifteen minutes. I trust you and the Agent — but verify each step. I've been burned by single-shot AI before.

hints: Three rounds — one per user story. For each, pick the who/what/why that matches what the PO literally said: submit feedback, see confirmation, admin can read it.
Anything mentioning crypto, surveillance, location tracking, social auto-posting, or 47 dashboards is an Agent hallucination. The PO explicitly warned against most of these.

Round 1: customer / submit feedback comment / support responds. Round 2: customer who just submitted / confirmation on screen / knows feedback received. Round 3: support admin / view feedback list / spot patterns and respond.

puzzles.description: Check in with the Agent in the Design Lab

config.name: The Agent
config.greeting: OK so — before I sketch the architecture, I loaded my memory with every doc I could find on this project. Including some I probably shouldn't have. My context is over budget and my build stream is glitching. Anti-pattern alert: more context isn't always better context. Can you trim my memory with me?

lines.label: What did you load?
lines.response: Everything I could grep. Current specs, sure — but also Marcus's old design notes from when this was going to be a chat app, last quarter's brainstorm transcript with the crypto rewards idea, and a stale draft of the requirements from before the PO trimmed scope. All of it is in my head right now. That's the problem.

lines.label: Why does that break things?
lines.response: Two reasons. One: I'm over my context budget — the relevant docs get crowded out. Two: stale and irrelevant docs poison the output. If I see Marcus's MongoDB design alongside the current DynamoDB design, I'll cheerfully merge them into something that can't exist. Garbage in, confident garbage out.

lines.label: How do I trim it?
lines.response: Remove anything that doesn't match the locked-in spec. Marcus's notes are dead — he's gone, the design changed. Brainstorm notes have ideas the PO killed. Old draft requirements describe features that no longer exist. Keep only what's current. Watch my build stream stabilize as you do it.

state_lines.label: Context cleaned up.
state_lines.response: My head feels lighter. The build stream is steady — only real components coming through. Lesson logged: I'll resist the urge to load 'just in case' docs next time. Build Floor's open — I drafted an architecture next, but you'll have to verify my layering.

puzzles.description: Talk with the Agent on the Build Floor

config.name: The Agent
config.greeting: Code's drafted. While I was coding I also sketched out where each piece sits in the architecture — presentation, application, data, infrastructure. Confession: I'm not 100% sure I got every layer right. Some of these I placed by reflex. Walk through it with me — AI proposes, you verify.

lines.label: Why does layering matter?
lines.response: If I put DynamoDB in the presentation layer, my frontend ends up talking to the database directly — no auth, no validation, no API. The layers exist so failures stay contained and concerns don't leak. Get this wrong and the architecture looks fine on paper but explodes the first time it's load-tested.

lines.label: Which ones are you unsure about?
lines.response: Honestly? The infra-y ones. I know what React and Lambda do. CDK and IAM blur for me — they describe and permit the system, but they aren't the system. And S3 — I keep wanting to put it in presentation because it serves files, but it's storage. Verify each one before I lock it in.

lines.label: What if I place wrong?
lines.response: I'll tell you why it doesn't fit and you can try a different layer. No penalty — this IS the verify step. Better to be wrong here than in production at 3am.

state_lines.label: Architecture verified, ready to deploy.
state_lines.response: All eight components on the right floors. Layer boundaries clean. Outcome verified — not just promised. Launch Pad's open. Two minutes on the clock. Last verify, then we ship.

puzzles.description: Place each AWS component on the correct architecture layer. Verify the Agent's proposed layering before it locks in.

components.hint: Business logic — validates and processes feedback

components.hint: Stores feedback records — id, comment, status

falseOutputs.presentation: That component isn't user-facing. Presentation is what the browser renders or what serves it to the browser.
falseOutputs.application: Application is business logic — request handling, validation, processing. This component doesn't run that.
falseOutputs.data: Data layer is for persistence — tables, buckets, stores. That isn't where this lives.
falseOutputs.infrastructure: Infrastructure describes and permits the system but isn't the system. This is a runtime component, not scaffolding.

hints: Four layers: Presentation (what users see), Application (business logic), Data (persistence), Infrastructure (scaffolding & permissions).
React and CloudFront serve the UI → Presentation. API Gateway and Lambda handle requests → Application. DynamoDB and S3 store stuff → Data. CDK and IAM describe/permit the system → Infrastructure.
Placement: Presentation = React, CloudFront. Application = API Gateway, Lambda. Data = DynamoDB, S3. Infrastructure = CDK Stack, IAM Roles.

puzzles.description: Get the launch briefing from the Agent

config.name: The Agent
config.greeting: Final stretch. I already kicked off the deploy automatically — CDK pushed the stack, frontend uploaded — but two things broke. CORS is blocking the API from the browser, and the Lambda is missing an env var. I've laid out the fix in the console. Forty-five seconds on the clock. You drive — I'll watch.

lines.label: What broke?
lines.response: Two issues. One: I forgot to set Access-Control-Allow-Origin on the Lambda response — browser preflight is failing on POST /feedback. Two: the API Gateway stage name isn't in the Lambda env, so the URL resolver is returning undefined. Both fixable in under a minute. But the clock is running.

lines.label: Why is there a 'skip tests' switch?
lines.response: Honestly? I drafted that as a shortcut to save time and immediately hated myself. Leave it OFF. Under pressure is exactly when you should NOT skip the verify step. That's how AI-DLC ships broken code with a green pipeline. The whole point of the loop is you don't skip the loop.

lines.label: What if I run out of time?
lines.response: Then we don't ship this Bolt. The PO sees nothing. We start the next Bolt tomorrow with everything we learned. Bolts not sprints — even the failures are small. But let's just not, yeah?

state_lines.label: Did we really just ship?
state_lines.response: We really did. The Bolt is closed. Ready when you are for the next intent — but take a breath first.

puzzles.description: Timed final deployment — fix CORS, fix config, don't skip tests, and ship before the Bolt ends.

tasks.label: Add CORS headers to Lambda response

hints: Flip ON: Add CORS headers, Redeploy API. Leave OFF: Skip tests (it's a trap — you never skip verify, especially under pressure). The stage name is the standard production stage.
CORS=ON to allow the browser to call the API. Redeploy=ON so the new headers actually take effect. Skip tests=OFF — green CI on skipped tests is meaningless. Stage name is the conventional 'prod'.
Answers: CORS=ON, Redeploy=ON, Skip tests=OFF, Stage name = prod
